questions.prompt: How does the domain-modeling note decide between value and identity for Money, Product and Subscription, and what does choosing a C# record settle, or not settle, about equality? Then explain how far Money's constructor validation reaches: can a Money value exist without the constructor running, and what exactly does the currency check verify?

keyPoints.text: Money is a value, so equality follows amount and currency.
keyPoints.quote: `Money` is a value: equality should follow amount and currency.

keyPoints.text: As a readonly record struct it gets value semantics and blocks ordinary property mutation.
keyPoints.quote: Its `readonly record struct` gives value semantics and prevents ordinary property mutation.

keyPoints.text: Product and Subscription have identity: two subscriptions with the same fields are still different subscriptions.
keyPoints.quote: two subscriptions with matching fields still represent different subscriptions.

keyPoints.text: A record is a language feature; it does not decide what equality means for the business.
keyPoints.quote: A record is a language feature, not a substitute for deciding what equality means in the business.

keyPoints.text: Constructor validation guards the normal construction paths but does not prove every representable value is valid.
keyPoints.quote: Constructor validation protects normal construction paths. It is not proof that every representable value is valid.

keyPoints.text: A struct always has a default value, so default(Money) exists even though the constructor rejects a missing currency.
keyPoints.quote: A struct has a default value even if its constructor rejects missing currency

keyPoints.text: The constructor only checks that the trimmed currency is three characters long; it does not check that they are letters.

questions.prompt: What does decimal give MeterForge and what does it leave undecided, how does the tiered rater apply rounding, and why must the rule be stated before arithmetic changes? Then explain what makes Invoice an aggregate: which rules it enforces on its lines, and what its read-only Lines collection does and does not protect.

keyPoints.text: decimal represents decimal fractions more directly than binary floating point, but it does not pick a rounding policy.
keyPoints.quote: `decimal` represents decimal fractions more directly than binary floating-point, but it does not choose a rounding policy

keyPoints.text: The tiered rater rounds each tier's charge and then adds the rounded charges.
keyPoints.quote: rounds each tier charge and then totals those charges.

keyPoints.text: Rounding per line and rounding only the final total can give different results.
keyPoints.quote: Rounding each line versus rounding only a final total can produce different results.

keyPoints.text: So the chosen rule is stated before any arithmetic is changed.
keyPoints.quote: State the chosen rule before changing arithmetic.

keyPoints.text: An aggregate groups state whose rules have to be maintained together.
keyPoints.quote: An aggregate groups state whose rules must be maintained together.

keyPoints.text: The invoice owns its lines, rejects negative or mixed-currency lines, and accepts no new lines once finalized.
keyPoints.quote: An invoice owns its lines, rejects negative or mixed-currency lines, and stops accepting new lines after finalization.

keyPoints.text: A read-only collection stops callers adding through it; whether the elements or referenced objects are mutable is a separate question.
keyPoints.quote: reason separately about whether the elements or any referenced objects remain mutable.

questions.prompt: What does Subscription.Pause() do beyond setting an enum, what can its Version increment show on its own, and where does a guarantee against two stored writers racing belong? Then explain how Invoice.Finalize handles the current time, what that makes testable, and when an injected clock is actually worth adding.

keyPoints.text: A state machine makes the allowed changes explicit.
keyPoints.quote: A state machine makes allowed changes explicit.

keyPoints.text: Pause checks the current state and increments the version, not just assigns an enum.
keyPoints.quote: `Subscription.Pause()` means more than assigning an enum: it checks the current state and increments the version.

keyPoints.text: The domain increment is evidence of change but cannot by itself prevent two stored writers racing.
keyPoints.quote: the domain increment alone cannot prevent two stored writers from racing.

keyPoints.text: That guarantee belongs at the mutation boundary, covered in the concurrency note.
keyPoints.quote: That guarantee belongs at the mutation boundary

keyPoints.text: Domain logic is easier to test when time and identity are passed in as values.
keyPoints.quote: Pure domain logic is easier to test when time and identity are supplied as values.

keyPoints.text: Finalize takes a timestamp and the API chooses the current time.
keyPoints.quote: `Invoice.Finalize(finalizedAt)` accepts a timestamp, while the API chooses the current time.

keyPoints.text: A test can then prove UTC normalization with a fixed value.
keyPoints.quote: This lets a test prove UTC normalization with a fixed value.

keyPoints.text: An injected clock helps when orchestration makes several time-dependent decisions; it need not be in every class.
keyPoints.quote: An injected clock is useful when orchestration has multiple time-dependent decisions; it need not appear in every class.
